paras: The lynching of Riley at Caddoa was the killing of a man named Riley by twelve to fifteen armed men at the Santa Fe railroad station at Caddoa, reported as in New Mexico, one night in mid-December 1882. Accused of murdering a tank tender, he was taken from the emigrant train, shot as he ran, and hanged from a telegraph pole in front of the passengers. The Wichita City Eagle printed the fullest account and complained that the Associated Press had published nothing about it.

Riley was accused of having murdered a railroad tank tender near Caddoa, a small station on the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe line. According to the Eagle, a stranger who boarded a few stations west of Caddoa had asked passengers to protect him because he feared men were on his track who would murder him.

When the emigrant train reached Caddoa at about 10:15 at night, armed men, about a dozen in the wire account and twelve or fifteen in the Eagle's, boarded it and searched the passengers' faces. Riley was found hiding in a box, which the Eagle described as an empty box car attached to the train, and was taken out to the platform. He protested his innocence and then tried to run, and after a few rods he was shot several times.

The men then carried him, bleeding, to a telegraph pole over which a lariat had been thrown and hoisted him about ten feet, firing their pistols into the body. Inside the cars women shrieked and fainted, and some passengers ran out onto the prairie with their children. The train then moved away and left the body hanging from the pole.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage, and none of the papers named the men or the murdered tank tender.

The story first appeared as an unsigned paragraph in a general news summary, printed by the Indian Chieftain at Vinita on December 22 and by the Iola Register and the Barbour County Index in Kansas on December 29. That version closed by saying that the screaming women and children and "the mob howling and firing made the scene a lively one." The Iola Register printed the place as "Caddo," while the other papers gave "Caddoa."

The Wichita City Eagle's separately written account, apparently drawn from passengers, was far more dramatic, calling the event "a terrible tragedy" and the men "infuriated lynchers" who were "yelling like fiends." The Eagle said every effort had been made to suppress the story, that the Associated Press had not published a line on it, and that without the passengers it would have gone unrecorded. None of the accounts gave Riley's race or described the killing in racial terms.

bases: A band of twelve to fifteen armed men took a man accused of murder off a train, shot him and hanged him from a telegraph pole (A1, A2).

Both accounts say a group of about a dozen (A1) or twelve to fifteen (A2) armed men with no stated authority shot and hanged Riley because he was accused of murdering a tank tender (A1, A2); A2 calls them 'lynchers'.
The wire paragraph (A1, reprinted A3, A4) and the separately written Wichita Eagle account (A2) agree on the train, the search, the box, the shooting and the hanging at a telegraph pole.

framing.detail: A short paragraph in news-summary columns, ending that the screaming and 'the mob howling and firing made the scene a lively one'.
The Wichita Eagle called it 'a terrible tragedy', described the 'infuriated lynchers' as 'yelling like fiends', and complained that the event had been suppressed.
